briefs.headline: Which Nifty is right for you?
briefs.deck: There is no single universally “best” index. However, history offers a useful reality check: diversification does not automatically mean lower risk
briefs.bodyText:
Imagine you decide to invest in equity via an index fund. But which market are you actually buying? The 50 biggest firms? The next 50 waiting in the wings? Or, a much broader basket of 500 firms? All three are called Nifty indices, but they can give your money very different rides. So, it’s worth asking a simple question: Which one to choose?
It matters because choosing an index fund is not simply a question of picking the one with more number of firms or the one with ‘bluechips’. Instead, you are choosing between how much of the market to own and where that exposure comes from.
Nifty 50
The Nifty 50 may give you exposure to 50 large firms but as of July 31, 2026 financial services alone accounted for 36.18%, healthcare 4.82% and power just 2.63% of the index. So, the real question for an investor is: Do you want the largest firms, the next tier of firms, a broader slice of market or a sector mix you are comfortable with?
What if you don’t want to bet on which part of the market will win? The Nifty 50 gives you exposure to 50 of the market’s largest firms. So, for an investor who wants to keep equity investing simple, it can be a ‘perfectly reasonable’ one-index approach. But there is an important question hiding beneath: are you comfortable owning mainly the firms that have already turned the market’s biggest or also firms that could become tomorrow’s ‘giants’? That is where the Nifty Next 50 enters the picture.
Nifty Next 50
If the Nifty 50 represents the established ‘giants’, the Nifty Next 50 takes you one step down the ladder, bringing in the next 50 companies outside the Nifty 50. That makes it an interesting middle ground: you are still investing in relatively large companies but moving beyond the market’s biggest names. For an investor who feels the Nifty 50 is too concentrated in today’s ‘giants’ but who does not want to straddle across the entire market, the Next 50 offers a different proposition. The next query is whether you want exposure to the next set of companies in the market-cap hierarchy or prefer the wider spread offered by the Nifty 500.
Nifty 500
What if you don’t want to pick a winner? This is where the Nifty 500 changes the scenario altogether. Instead of deciding whether the market’s biggest companies or the next tier will do better, you are spreading your exposure much further across the Indian equity market. That can appeal to an investor who does not want to make a call on which segment of the market will lead over the next 10 or 20 years.
The trade-off is equally important: you are also accepting exposure to companies beyond the large-cap universe, which can make the ride different from a Nifty 50 fund. In simple terms, Nifty 50 asks you to back the ‘giants’; Nifty Next 50 gives you the ‘climbers’; Nifty 500 lets you own a much larger part of the race.
Which one to choose?
There is no single universally “best” index. However, history offers a useful reality check: diversification does not automatically mean lower risk. In NSE Indices’ February 2026 Riskometer assessment, all three indices were classified as “Very High” risk, but the scores rose from 5.33 for Nifty 50 to 5.43 for Nifty Next 50 and 5.60 for Nifty 500.
So, while Nifty 500 gives you a much wider slice of the market, it has not been the least risky of the three by this measure. The choice, therefore, is less about finding a “safe” index and more about deciding how much market breadth and volatility you are prepared to accept.
(The writer is an NISM & CRISIL-certified Wealth Manager and certified in NISM’s Research Analyst module)

briefs.headline: Why gold should form 10% of investment portfolio
briefs.deck: Most investors think of portfolio in terms of equity and fixed income but buying gold is not a speculative add-on, it is a structural building block of a well-constructed portfolio
briefs.bodyText:
Most investors think of portfolio in terms of equity and fixed income. Gold is an afterthought. That approach misses the point. Gold deserves a deliberate, planned allocation of about 10% of every portfolio and here is why.
A diversifier, not a bet
Long-term data shows gold behaves differently from equity and fixed income in most situations. When equity markets are under stress, gold tends to hold up or even gain. When bond yields rise sharply on inflation worries, gold does well since it is seen as a hedge against currency depreciation. This is the essence of diversification - you don’t want all assets moving in the same direction at the same time.
If you run a portfolio with equity and fixed income and allocate 10% to gold, the math works out in your favour as the overall portfolio volatility drops as gold price movements are not synchronised with the other two asset classes. Risk-adjusted or volatility-adjusted return improves. This is how portfolio construction works when you combine assets that do not move in lockstep. You are adding gold as it smoothens the ride.
Global central banks have been briskly adding gold to reserves.
Central bank buying
Sanctions, trade tensions and a more fragmented world order have made many central banks wary of holding all reserves in U.S. Treasuries. Gold held within a country’s own vaults does not carry counterparty risk the way a government bond does. This shift by central banks has been one of the steadiest sources of demand for gold over the past four years.
No trend breaking
Gold has corrected meaningfully from a peak earlier this year. Prices had run up too far too quickly, and some of that froth had to come off. What matters more is if the long-term uptrend is intact. Chartists tracking gold have a technical support line and even after this correction, that line has not been broken. A correction within an intact uptrend is very different from a trend reversal.
Rupee depreciation
Gold price is quoted in U.S. dollars and set daily by the London Bullion Market Association. The price in India is that global dollar price converted into rupees. Over the long run, the rupee had depreciated against the dollar and is likely to continue so. Every time the rupee weakens, it adds to rupee-denominated return from gold over and above whatever the dollar price of gold itself does. This is a tailwind that many investors overlook.
U.S. Fed rate and gold
Gold has an inverse relationship with the U.S. dollar (USD). When the USD strengthens, gold in dollar terms tends to soften and vice versa. The U.S. Federal Reserve is likely to raise interest rates which will act as a headwind for gold.
However, there is a limit to how much the Fed can hike as the U.S. is sitting on a huge pile of debt and higher rates mean higher cost of servicing it. At some point, the arithmetic of debt servicing and growth of economy forces a pause/reversal, in the rate cycle. Investors should see dollar-gold relationship as cyclical on gold’s prospects.
Several routes
There are several routes to gold. Sovereign Gold Bonds, offering 2.5% annual interest on top of gold’s price appreciation are no longer issued afresh but existing bonds can be bought and sold in the secondary market. Gold Exchange Traded Funds are an evergreen option — you need a demat and trading account with a broker and can buy/sell units. If you do not have a demat account, Gold Funds from mutual funds (MFs) serve the same purpose and you can invest via regular MF folio, including SIP.
More recently, a new avenue has opened up: Electronic Gold Receipts or EGRs. These are SEBI-regulated securities representing direct ownership of physical gold held in accredited vaults. You buy/sell EGRs on the stock exchange, just like a share and they sit in demat account. Each EGR is a receipt against a specific quantity of physical gold with the option to convert holdings into gold bars/coins via withdrawal request subject to charges/taxes. EGRs are available in small denominations making them accessible even to small investors. For those who want transparency of exchange-based pricing along with the comfort of an actual claim on physical gold, EGRs are worth considering as part of the 10% allocation. Whichever route, the underlying point is: gold is not a speculative add-on, it is a structural building block of a well-constructed portfolio.
(Joydeep Sen is a corporate trainer [financial markets] and author)

stories.headline: England trounce Pakistan by 194 runs to win series
stories.deck: Ollie Robinson was Pakistan's chief tormentor again as he took four wickets for 24 to go ‌with the four for 11 he bagged in the ‌first ⁠innings, taking his total in the two tests ⁠to 16.
stories.bodyText:
England beat Pakistan by 194 runs in the second test and sealed their first home test series victory for two years as they bowled the visitors out for 194 at Lord's on Sunday (August 30, 2026).
The outcome was a formality as Pakistan were reduced to 14-3 before lunch, chasing an unlikely target of 389, but Saud Shakeel provided some resistance with a magnificent fighting 97.
Ollie Robinson was Pakistan's chief tormentor again as he took four wickets for 24 to go with the four for 11 he bagged in the first innings, taking his total in the two tests to 16.
After a rain-hit Saturday, England resumed on day four on 177-7 but were all out for 208 after Pakistan quick Mohammad Abbas helped mop up to finish with five wickets.
Robinson removed Azan Awais lbw with a delivery that nipped back off a length and three balls later produced a stunning delivery that hit the top of Abdullah Shafique's off stump, leaving Pakistan reeling on 7-2.
There was no respite before lunch for Pakistan as captain Babar Azam tried to fend off a vicious Jofra Archer bouncer but could only edge it via his helmet to Jordan Cox at third slip.
Shan Masood and Shakeel dug in though and at least steered Pakistan to their highest score of the series so far.
Robinson removed Masood for 26 after lunch, but Shakeel provided some afternoon entertainment as he struck 13 fours and two sixes in a brilliant knock.
There was genuine disappointment around the ground when he fell three runs short of a deserved century, trying to launch Josh Tongue over the deep square leg boundary but picking out Harry Brook, before walking off to a hearty reception.
With Pakistan opener Imam-ul-Haq again unable to bat because of an injury sustained in the field on Thursday, England only needed nine wickets to finish the contest and Tongue completed the victory by dismissing Mohammad Ali.
The third and final test will start at Edgbaston on September 9.

stories.headline: England’s pace quartet fires again as Robinson-Archer combo seals series win over Pakistan
stories.deck: England supporters are getting excited about having four seamers who are winning test matches with a home Ashes series against Australia on the horizon
stories.bodyText:
Long may it continue, England seam bowler Ollie Robinson said.
And there's the rub.
Robinson was talking about how successful his new-ball partnership with Jofra Archer was working out. In harness together for the first time in test cricket, they have taken 24 of Pakistan’s 38 possible wickets in the ongoing series.
They are a big reason England clinched the series 2-0 at Lord's on Sunday with a day and a game to spare.
The change bowlers, Josh Tongue and Gus Atkinson, have come off helping Manchester win the Hundred competition and claimed the other 14 Pakistan wickets.
It's a pace attack that is exciting England supporters, who have fingers crossed that the four quicks can stick together for the home Ashes series against Australia in less than 10 months.
But that's a long time for any player and the foursome has yet to be truly tested. Pakistan has underwhelmed and was struggling before it undertook its first tour of England in six years. The loss at Lord's was its 10th in its last 11 away tests. The third and last test starts on Sept. 9 at Edgbaston.
Ironically, the retirement of former captain and allrounder Ben Stokes brought the four seamers together in the first post-Bazball series for England.
New captain Joe Root said after they won the first test at Leeds by an innings that the four “do not know how good they can be.” At Lord’s, Root admitted he's still trying to figure it out, too.
“It's just getting used to it, seeing how it works, having a good understanding of it for me as captain, for them as bowlers and for us as a side,” he said. “The more that happens I think the better for it we'll be.”
Robinson has been the series standout with 8-80 in Leeds and 8-35 at Lord's. He was brought out of exile in June after two years and then got injured and didn't finish the series defeat to New Zealand.
He's credited his fortune to bowling in tandem with Archer, who regularly bowls over 90 mph (145 kph) and has hit 95 mph (153 kph). Archer puts batters in a foxhole and when they poke their heads up Robinson knocks them out.
“The four-man attack we've got, I think it's going to be very successful,” Robinson said.
"My role doesn't change, it allows me to be a bit more defensive if anything. I can just hold and be patient and not try to punch through the batters. Jof and the other guys can then bowl rapid and break it up at the other end.
“It's quite a nice pairing to open the bowling with, someone bowling that quickly and swinging the ball the other way from me. Long may it continue.”
Root praised Robinson, who has been named the player of the match in all three of his tests this summer.
“He's bowling beautifully,” Root said. "If you asked good questions of guys' defense for long period of times with a wicket that gives you assistance, you're going to cause problems. He's been phenomenal, relentless.
"It's a good contrast with the guys on the other end as well — you've got 90 mph from the other three. Even Gus today bowling 90 mph at times, it’s really impressive stuff. I think it's a really well balanced attack.
“The more they can complement each other's skill sets, it's only going to be a good thing for us moving forward.”

stories.headline: Deepti Sharma scripts history! Stunning 3/0 makes her world’s leading T20I wicket-taker
stories.deck: Deepti Sharma has made history by becoming the leading wicket-taker in Women's T20I cricket, demonstrating her exceptional skills with a remarkable three wickets for no runs in a thrilling match against Thailand in Dubai. With Shafali Verma’s explosive 64 earlier contributing to a solid foundation, India celebrated a resounding 94-run victory, setting an exciting tone for their Asia Cup campaign.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Deepti Sharma
 scripted history on Sunday, producing one of the most remarkable bowling spells in Women’s T20I cricket to become the highest wicket-taker in the format as India began their Women’s T20 Asia Cup campaign with a thumping 94-run victory over Thailand in Dubai.
Playing her landmark 150th T20I, Deepti claimed three wickets without conceding a single run from seven deliveries, taking her career tally to 171 wickets and moving past Thailand’s Thipatcha Putthawong, who took one wicket in the match to reach 170 wickets.
The veteran all-rounder first drew level with Putthawong when she took two wickets in the ninth over to leave Thailand reeling at 44/6. She returned in the 17th over and struck with her very first delivery, dismissing wicketkeeper-batter Nannapat Koncharoenkai to complete a stunning 3/0.
Thailand were eventually bowled out for just 65 in 16.1 overs, giving India a winning start to their campaign.
Deepti enters record books with sensational spell
Deepti's achievement was made even more remarkable by the fact that she became the first Indian bowler to claim three or more wickets without conceding a run in a Women's T20I. Overall, there have now been 26 such spells in the format.
Her figures of 3/0 are also the best for an Indian bowler taking at least three wickets in a T20I. 
Renuka Singh previously held the record for the fewest runs conceded with 3/5 against Sri Lanka in Sylhet in 2022.
Deepti's three wickets also took her past Putthawong at the top of the global wicket-taking charts. She now has 171 wickets, followed by Putthawong on 170, Rwanda's Henriette Ishimwe on 164 and England's Sophie Ecclestone on 154.
The landmark came on a memorable day for Deepti, who had earlier become only the third Indian after Harmanpreet Kaur and Smriti Mandhana to reach 150 T20I appearances.
Most wickets in Women’s T20Is
- 171* - Deepti Sharma (IND-W)
- 170 - Thipatcha Putthawong (THA-W)
- 164 - Henriette Ishimwe (RWA-W)
- 154 - Sophie Ecclestone (ENG-W)
- 153 - Kary Chan (HKG-W)
- 153 - Onnicha Kamchomphu (THA-W)
Shafali's fireworks set up India's win
Before Deepti's record-breaking intervention, Shafali Verma had provided India with a flying start. The opener smashed 64 from 36 balls, hitting eight fours and three sixes, and brought up her 19th T20I half-century from just 26 deliveries.
India raced past 100 in 10 overs and appeared set for a total in excess of 200. However, Thailand fought back through leg-spinner 
Suleeporn Laomi
, whose variations triggered a dramatic Indian collapse.
India slipped from 108/2 to 137/9, losing seven wickets for only 29 runs. Laomi finished with impressive figures of 3/26, including the wickets of Shafali and Richa Ghosh in successive deliveries. Off-spinner Sunida Chaturongrattana added 2/31.
Smriti Mandhana had earlier scored 19 from 10 balls before being run out by a direct hit from Aphisara Suwanchonrathi. Pratika Rawal, making her T20I debut in place of injured Jemimah Rodrigues, contributed 22 from 18 balls before Laomi cleaned her up.
Despite the collapse, India managed 159/9, with Kranti Gaud's unbeaten 15 off eight balls providing a late boost.
Least runs conceded for a 3-plus wicket haul for IND-W in a T20I
- 3/0 - Deepti Sharma vs THA-W, Dubai, 2026
- 3/5 - Renuka Singh vs SL-W, Sylhet, 2022
- 3/6 - Pooja Vastrakar vs MAS-W, Kuala Lumpur, 2018
- 3/6 - Titas Sadhu vs SL-W, Hangzhou, 2023
- 3/6 - Radha Yadav vs SA-W, Chennai, 2024
Thailand's chase never got going. Kranti Gaud and Nandani Sharma removed the openers early, while Shree Charani and Deepti then dismantled the middle order. Charani finished with 2/10 and Nandani took 3/18.
Nannapat offered the only significant resistance with 41, but Deepti ended her stay with the first ball of her final over.
The comprehensive win gives India two points to begin their Group A campaign. They next face Hong Kong on Thursday.

stories.headline: Asia Cup: Shafali, Deepti help India seal convincing 94-run win over Thailand
stories.deck: India kicked off their Women's T20 Asia Cup with an impressive 94-run triumph against Thailand. Shafali Verma ignited the innings with her electrifying batting, laying a robust foundation for the team. The bowlers showcased their prowess, limiting Thailand to a modest score. Highlighting the match, Deepti Sharma reached a remarkable milestone, claiming the title of leading wicket-taker in women's…
stories.bodyText:
India opened their Women’s T20 Asia Cup campaign with a convincing 94-run victory over Thailand on Sunday, overcoming a late batting collapse with a dominant bowling performance.
Shafali sets platform, India stumble late
India looked on course for a huge total after Shafali Verma smashed 64 off 36 balls, hitting eight fours and three sixes. Alongside debutant Pratika Rawal, who made 22 off 18, Shafali helped India race to 101/2 after 10 overs.
Smriti Mandhana contributed 19 off 10 balls, but was run out after hitting four boundaries. However, India lost their way dramatically after reaching 108/2, slipping to 137/9 as Thailand’s bowlers fought back. Leg-spinner 
Suleeporn Laomi
 was the standout performer with 3/26. Kranti Gaud, unbeaten on 15, helped India push the total to 159/9.
India’s bowlers run riot
Thailand’s chase never really got going as India’s bowlers produced a clinical display. Kranti Gaud and Nandni Sharma struck early to remove Thailand’s openers before India’s spinners took control. Nandni finished with three wickets, while 
Deepti Sharma
 produced an extraordinary spell, taking 3/0 in 1.1 overs.
Deepti’s three-wicket haul also saw her become the leading wicket-taker in women’s T20I cricket. Thailand struggled to cope with India’s attack and were eventually bowled out for just 65, with Nannapat Koncharoenkai providing the only significant resistance.
Koncharoenkai fights lone battle
Koncharoenkai top-scored for Thailand with 41 off 48 balls, including five fours. She remained at the crease until the final wicket, but lacked support as wickets continued to fall around her. India ultimately wrapped up the contest with a 94-run victory, making a strong start to their Asia Cup campaign.

briefs.headline: Germany win record-equalling fourth World Cup, defeat Spain by solitary goal
briefs.deck: With this, Germany has now become the most successful team in the history of the Men's Hockey World Cup, along with Pakistan
briefs.bodyText:
Winning once was good, Germany had to do it one more time. An efficient German side edged Spain 1-0 in a cagey final to claim a second successive men’s World Cup title on Sunday.
It was by no means a classic at the Belifus Arena. The finalists had derailed co-host Belgium’s journey to a home World championship decider and both boasted the meanest tournament defence. It was reflected in a tightly-fought encounter, making it a hard watch for the supporters dominated by neutrals.
Not that Germany would have minded one bit. As when it mattered, late in the third quarter, Michel Struthoff kept his calm, rounding off the Spain ‘keeper Luis Calzado to put the ball into the net for the decisive goal.

It was a massive achievement for head coach Andre Henning, who oversaw a massive transition with only nine returnees from the 2023 group.
Germany looked dangerous on the counter, breaking forward from deeper areas, using the wings. After just 90 seconds, Benedikt Schwarzhaupt’s drag-flick was kicked out by Calzado, but it wasn’t any indication of things to come. Spain’s defence, led by Jordi Bonastre, guarded its circle, not allowing Germany to get into shot-taking positions.
Spain, meanwhile, struggled to find its rhythm until the second quarter, and didn’t test Jean-Paul Danneberg as much as it would have liked.
Spain had three short corners in the third quarter but Pepe Cunill and Marc Miralles fired wide of the post. In the third quarter, even though Spain had the best of the exchanges, Germany remained dangerous on the counter. But a rare defensive lapse proved costly for the Iberian nation, which Struthoff capitalised on.

briefs.headline: Drawn to defeat: On India’s chances in the ICC World Test Championship
briefs.deck: India is now in a must-win situation in the Test Championship cycle
briefs.bodyText:
This was a triumph that ironically suffered the after-effects of a loss. India’s 1-0 series victory in the two-Test outing recently in Sri Lanka, in normal circumstances, would have been seen as a positive. However, in the race for key points in the ICC World Test Championship (WTC) cycle, the ideal India-centric result would have been a clean sweep at 2-0. But with Dhananjaya de Silva’s men thwarting India’s bid for a win in the second Test at Colombo’s Sinhalese Sports Club Ground, and forcing a draw, the visitors continue to occupy the fifth slot in the WTC rankings. It is a position one below Bangladesh after the eastern neighbour secured a 1-1 draw against Australia in the series Down Under. If a WTC final berth has to be secured then India has to do extremely well away against New Zealand and at home against Australia, and then hope that the various permutations cropping up will be favourable. Shubman Gill’s men find themselves in this piquant situation due to their vulnerability at home, having lost a Test series to South Africa last year. The transition angst within the Indian unit is yet to abate following the exit of R. Ashwin, Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma. Slowly, new heroes are emerging and the results could improve.
Stepping into the Emerald Isle and hamstrung by the injured Jasprit Bumrah’s absence, India did its homework. A warm-up fixture was won, while some of its players had earlier turned out for India A against Sri Lanka A and were ready. When the series commenced with the first Test at picturesque Galle, India led from the front and won by 165 runs to secure a 1-0 lead. Devdutt Padikkal’s 167 and 44 led the run charts and most importantly it also meant that the critical number three spot in the batting order had found an apt occupant for now. This is the same position that in the past had featured pedigreed men such as Dilip Vengsarkar, Rahul Dravid and Cheteshwar Pujara. Left-arm spinner Manav Suthar too did well and his classical mode is a throwback to a gentle past. Sri Lanka’s brief resistance hinged on Sonal Dinusha, who registered a ton. Soon he would become an immovable personality at the batting crease and India learnt it the hard way at Colombo. His twin hundreds helped Sri Lanka erase the ignominy of suffering a follow-on and also survive a tense final day to wrest a draw. The conclusion felt like a victory for the host and India is now placed in a must-win corner in its future Tests.

briefs.headline: Barcelona's Yamal getting back to 'top level': Flick
briefs.deck: The 19-year-old struggled in Barca's first match of the season at Elche but improved against Athletic Bilbao in the second, albeit without finding the net
briefs.bodyText:
Barcelona coach Hansi Flick indicated teenage star Lamine Yamal is finding his way back to his "top level" ahead of Monday's (August 31, 2026) La Liga clash against Rayo Vallecano.
The 19-year-old struggled in Barca's first match of the season at Elche but improved against Athletic Bilbao in the second, albeit without finding the net.
Flick said the Spanish World Cup winner is returning to his best, which Yamal has not hit since suffering a hamstring injury in April.
The winger returned at the World Cup but, despite Spain's success, had limited individual impact at the tournament.
"I know everyone is worried about how Lamine is, how he is doing. And of course, look at his situation: he played in a World Cup after a huge injury," Flick told reporters on Sunday (August 30).

briefs.headline: Dhruv Jurel — a blend of versatility and fortitude
briefs.deck: The decision-makers continued to invest their belief in him and the batter has responded in style. Towards the end of June, he was a part of the India ‘A’ squad that travelled on the ‘shadow’ tour of Sri Lanka for two unofficial ‘Tests’
briefs.bodyText:
Even before November 1999, a host of exceptional wicketkeeper-batters had graced the international scene, not least India’s own Farokh Engineer and the wonderful Andy Flower from Zimbabwe. But from the time a left-hander from Western Australia stormed the Test firmament at the Gabba in Brisbane nearly 27 years back with a bruising 81 on debut, against a shell-shocked Pakistani outfit, wicketkeeper-batters have been looked at in an entirely different vein.
Adam Gilchrist rewrote the dynamics of Test batsmanship. He was a destructive opener in limited-overs cricket long before he played his first Test, and reeled off numerous wondrous knocks, including in the final of the 50-over 2007 World Cup when, with a squash ball for company, he bludgeoned his way to 149 against Mahela Jaywardene’s Sri Lanka in a decisive effort that took Australia to a hat-trick of titles. But it was in the red-ball game that Gilchrist set stall as a pioneer, providing not just meaningful heft to the Australian batting but scoring runs at such a furious clip that opponents were often ducking, unsuccessfully, for cover.
For the most part of his glittering career that encompassed 96 Tests, the left-hander had the luxury of batting behind a grand top six that used different methodologies to subjugate bowling attacks in all parts of the world. The sight of Gilchrist, the destroyer supreme, striding in purposefully at No. 7, was dispiriting or exhilarating, depending on which side of the fence one was. Gilchrist seldom disappointed; when he scored his runs, he did so with not just panache and chutzpah but also with a violent streak that damaged bowling figures as well as egos. How could anyone bat with such unchecked aggression at No. 7? How could someone fuse a no-holds-barred approach with such consistency (as an average of 47.60 at a strike-rate of 81.95 will unequivocally testify to)?
Gold standard
Gilchrist will remain the gold standard among wicketkeeper-batters, the platform from which the likes of Mahendra Singh Dhoni, more than anyone else, launched himself into the stratosphere. Gilchrist’s towering presence kept an entire generation – or more – of Aussie stumper-batters out of international reckoning. India, however, found a judicious balance; while Dhoni’s aggression in front of the stumps and his brilliance behind it precluded a dynamic new force breaking through, India were compelled to find a place, if only as a specialist batter, for Dinesh Karthik, the ebullient little right-hander from Chennai who was more than good enough to hold his own as a batter.
Karthik wasn’t the first Indian gloveman to play as a specialist batter. Nearly four decades before him, Budhi Kunderan donned that role, even opening the batting in England in 1967 alongside designated wicketkeeper Engineer. A couple of decades on, Chandrakant Pandit played as a middle-order bat with Kiran More slotting in as the wicketkeeper. Such was Karthik’s great natural ability – which he didn’t maximise, he will acknowledge – that in the Dhoni era, India fielded him as a full-fledged opener overseas, and with no little success. Alongside Wasim Jaffer, Karthik formed an excellent opening combine in Bangladesh and England in 2007, bringing up his only Test ton across the border and bettering that effort by emerging as India’s highest scorer in England, when they last won a Test series there by a slender 1-0 margin.
Karthik played his last eight Tests down the order, sometimes when Dhoni wasn’t available (including through retirement) and he donned the big gloves, and at others when he played alongside the Jharkhandi as a pure batter. Just one half-century in his last 14 Test innings meant he played the last of his 26 Tests in August 2018; his Test average of 25 was decidedly underwhelming, given his supreme gift as a batter, but that can happen when one is overeager and anxious to not just justify their selection but also state their case for a longer rope.
India now have a profusion of excellent wicketkeeper-batters across formats – Rishabh Pant, of course, tops that chart, especially when it comes to the red-ball variant, but there are a host of others that can’t be ignored. Among them are Sanju Samson and Ishan Kishan, exclusive when it comes to the white-ball version. And Dhruv Jurel, the 25-year-old from Agra whose first Test cap came as a wicketkeeper against England in Rajkot in February 2024 when Pant was out after his horrific road accident of 14 months previously and KS Bharat had played himself out of the XI with poor efforts in the first two Tests in Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam respectively.
The generational talent that Pant is, he kept almost exclusively from the time he made his Test debut in Nottingham in August 2018 and made a stunning 114 in his third appearance at the Oval till his single-car accident in December 2022 when India were suddenly forced to scramble for a replacement. Bharat, from Andhra, won the early nod for the home Tests against Australia in February 2023 and donned the big gloves in the final of the World Test Championship against the same opponents that June. KL Rahul was nominated the first-choice stumper for the two Tests in South Africa towards the end of the year, more to provide stability and class to the lower order in a line-up from which very few had played in South Africa previously. Bharat reclaimed his spot behind the sticks against England at home and played himself out of the XI following scores of 41, 28, 17 and 6 which meant that in seven Tests and 12 innings, he only averaged 20.09, a definite no-no given that the wicketkeeper’s was no longer a single-discipline specialised slot.
Out went the call to Jurel for the third Test in Rajkot with the series finely poised at 1-1, and it was immediately apparent that India had hit upon a gold mine. The right-hander made a poised 46 on debut, and upped the ante in the next match with scores of 90 and 39 not out, the first ensuring that India didn’t end up conceding a massive lead and the second taking them home in a tense run-chase when he and Shubman Gill put on 72 for the unfinished sixth-wicket stand.
This was in February 2024, when one wasn’t sure when Pant would be available for selection though in a characteristic show of gumption and guts, the stocky left-hander was far ahead of the timelines the doctors had tentatively outlined for a possible comeback to competitive cricket. Pant was ready for international cricket in September that year, making a remarkable recovery from a series of potentially life-threatening injuries to smash 109 on his comeback Test in Chennai against Bangladesh. Suddenly, Jurel faced an uncertain future. Despite an impressive start to his Test career, he had to bow before the irrepressible force that Pant was, though it was always on the cards that he could slot in alongside Pant, if not necessarily ahead of him.
In six of his last nine Tests, Jurel has occupied a specialist batter’s position between No. 4 and No. 8 (and that only because Akash Deep was employed as a nightwatchman at the Oval last August). On the three occasions when was the designated wicketkeeper, Pant was unavailable through injury after breaking his right foot in the Manchester Test against England in July last year. Despite the vast array of batting riches at India’s disposal, head coach Gautam Gambhir has identified in Jurel a dependable batting option, and the man from Uttar Pradesh has comprehensively justified that faith with two hundreds and a fifty in those nine Tests and 15 innings.
Jurel’s coming-of-age moment, if it can be called that, transpired in Ahmedabad last October with Pant still to recover from the broken foot. In India’s only innings against West Indies, he uncorked an excellent 125, then followed it up with 44 in the next Test in Delhi. With Pant returning to action against South Africa in November, Jurel continued on as a batter alone though like the rest of his colleagues, he had a series to forget with outings of 14, 13, 0 and 2 in a disastrous 0-2 result that has comprehensively dented India’s hopes of making a third WTC final in four cycles.
But instead of pressing the panic button and looking elsewhere, the decision-makers continued to invest their belief in him and Jurel has responded in style. Towards the end of June, he was a part of the India ‘A’ squad that travelled on the ‘shadow’ tour of Sri Lanka for two unofficial ‘Tests’, ostensibly at the insistence of Gambhir because of his felicity against the turning ball. Jurel warmed up nicely for the Test series to follow with scores of 141 not out, 14 and 53, and it was no surprise that he was picked for the first Test in Galle, when he weighed in with 51 and 7 in a winning cause.
In Colombo last week, Jurel went one better with an unbeaten 115 during which he brought his technical expertise and his mental fortitude into play. He also kept wickets for a while when Pant was recovering from a blow to his right shoulder sustained while batting, and when he went back to the outfield, took a terrific running catch from point to get rid of Lahiru Kumara in Sri Lanka’s first innings. At every stage in every role, he has looked the part, making his presence felt with total commitment and a never-say-die spirit without seeking recourse to the flashy and the flamboyant.
Jurel was chosen for Sri Lanka for his ability to play spin with finesse, and it is hard now to see him being overlooked during the November Test tour of New Zealand where the challenges for batters will be vastly different. At No. 6, behind Pant, he has the technique to tackle the second new ball if that is what he is confronted with. Ravindra Jadeja behind him in the batting order and the possible return of Washington Sundar from injury mean he is a right-handed option around a plethora of left-handers, and while that alone can’t be a qualification, he has shown that he can hold his own against bowling of any kind in any conditions.
India are fortunate that in Jurel, they have a three-in-one cricketer with his entire future ahead of him. As a batting average of 40.68 from 12 Tests proves, he is every bit deserving of the show of confidence. A place in the starting XI in Wellington in November is no more than he deserves; one can rest assured that Jurel will be short on neither preparation nor fire when ‘Play’ is called at the Basin Reserve.

briefs.headline: Deepti's record spell powers India to 94-run rout of Thailand in women's Asia Cup opener
briefs.deck: The flamboyant opener smashed eight fours and three sixes in her 36-ball knock before Thailand's spinners, led by Suleeporn Laomi's three-wicket haul, triggered an inexplicable Indian collapse to restrict the seven-time champions to 159/9
briefs.bodyText:
Shafali Verma's belligerent 64 set the tone before Deepti Sharma's record-breaking three-wicket burst without conceding a run powered India to a thumping 94-run win over Thailand in their Women's T20 Asia Cup opener here on Sunday.
The flamboyant opener smashed eight fours and three sixes in her 36-ball knock before Thailand's spinners, led by Suleeporn Laomi's three-wicket haul, triggered an inexplicable Indian collapse to restrict the seven-time champions to 159/9.
But the total proved more than enough as Thailand folded for 65 in 16.1 overs, with Deepti, playing in her landmark 150th T20I, claiming three wickets in seven balls without conceding a run to take her tally to 171 wickets, becoming the outright leading wicket-taker in Women's T20I cricket.
The 29-year-old veteran allrounder, who became the only the third Indian after Harmanpreet Kaur and Smriti Mandhana to reach the 150 T20I landmark, had earlier drawn level with Thailand's Thipatcha Putthawong at 170 wickets after taking two wickets in the ninth over to leave Thailand reeling at 44/6.
She returned in the 17th over and struck with her very first delivery to dismiss wicketkeeper-batter Nannapat Koncharoenkai, who had offered Thailand some resistance with a 41-run knock to complete a sensational spell.
Seamers Kranti Goud (1/26) and Nandani Sharma (3/18) removed both Thailand openers inside four overs before left-arm spinner Shree Charani (2/10) and Deepti strangled the chase.
Charani struck twice in successive overs before Deepti produced a double-wicket maiden to virtually end Thailand's hopes, reducing them to 44/6 inside nine overs.
India, despite their late collapse with the bat, completed a comprehensive victory to begin their Asia Cup campaign in emphatic fashion from Group A.
India next face Hong Kong on Thursday.
For Thailand, this was their first loss after two matches, having begun their campaign with six-run win over Hong Kong on Friday.
Asked to bat, India cruised past 100-run mark in 10 overs, with Shafali smashing her 19th T20I fifty off just 26 balls.
The opener hit eight fours and three sixes in her 36-ball 64 (8x4, 3x6) and looked set to propel India to a 200-plus total before the innings unravelled.
India lost four wickets for 21 runs as Laomi's variations, drift and flight exposed the middle order.
The 28-year-old leg-spinner finished with 3/26, including two wickets in two balls off Shafali and Richa Ghosh, while off-spinner Sunida Chaturongrattana claimed 2/31.
India had a flying start with Smriti Mandhana (19; 10b) taking on the attack before a brilliant direct hit from Aphisara Suwanchonrathi cut short the Indian vice-captain's innings.
Thereafter Shafali took on left-arm spinner Thipatcha Putthawong with successive boundaries before advancing down the track to hit Sunida for a six and a four.
She then charged Laomi and cleared long-off for a six and raced to her fifty.
Laomi then struck against the run of play, removing Pratika Rawal, who was cleaned up for 22 off 18 balls by a delivery that darted back in and crashed into her leg stump.
The ODI specialist Rawal was drafted into the playing XI at No 3 for her T20I debut in place of the injured Jemimah Rodrigues.
Momentum was still with India with 100/2 at the halfway stage.
But captain Harmanpreet Kaur fell for five, edging a sweep to give Putthawong her 170th T20I wicket.
The biggest blow came in the following over when Laomi struck twice in two balls.
Shafali attempted to take on a slower, tossed-up delivery but chipped a return catch to the bowler.
Richa then fell for a duck, driving another full delivery straight to extra cover.
Deepti was run out for five as Laomi capped a superb spell with a sharp throw.
Sunida then compounded India's troubles in the 17th over, dismissing Bharti Fulmali for 13 and Prema Rawat for six in the space of four balls.
At 137/9 in 17.2 overs India were in danger of being bowled out before Kranti Gaud provided a late flourish with an unbeaten 15 off eight balls to take India past the 150-run mark.

briefs.headline: Hockey World Cup: Germany retain crown after Struthoff’s strike sinks Spain 1-0
briefs.deck: In a thrilling final, Germany's men's hockey team triumphed over Spain to clinch their fourth World Cup title. The match pivoted on a brilliant goal from Michel Struthoff in the 44th minute, while goalkeeper Jean-Paul Danneberg's outstanding saves protected Germany's slim victory. Despite Spain controlling the ball and creating numerous opportunities, they were left wanting as they failed to…
briefs.bodyText:
Germany’s men’s hockey team were crowned world champions after beating Spain at Belfius Hockey Arena in Wavre, Belgium, on Sunday.
They successfully defended their World Cup crown for the second time in history and became only the second team, after Pakistan, to win the title four times. Coached by André Henning, Germany had lost to Spain in the second round earlier in the tournament. But they came out on top when it mattered most, securing a 1-0 victory courtesy of Michel Struthoff’s goal in the 44th minute.
Against the run of play, Germany went on the offensive and released Struthoff inside the semi-circle. He did brilliantly to guide the ball past Spanish goalkeeper Luis Calzado on the run.
Struthoff had another opportunity to double Germany’s lead in the final quarter but could not keep his shot on target this time. It ultimately did not matter as Germany held on to lift the trophy.
Speaking after the match, Germany captain Christopher Ruhr, who was named Player of the Match, was delighted to prove the doubters wrong.
“I think everyone said, ‘Ah, the Germans this year? Nah, they won’t be there.’ Everyone focused on the other teams, but we showed what we’re capable of and played an amazing competition,” Ruhr told the broadcaster.
“It was unbelievably tough. I think Spain played a hell of a tournament. We always struggle against Spain — they’re a tough side, and they played a really good game today. We had the lucky end.”
Spain indeed dominated large parts of the game, recording nine shots on goal, 24 circle entries and four penalty corners. But Germany defended resolutely to deny Spain their maiden World Cup title.
But their victory would not have been possible without the heroic efforts of goalkeeper Jean-Paul Danneberg. He made several superb saves throughout the match, including a brilliant stop with his left hand to deny Borja Lacalle from the left. His presence also forced the Spaniards to go wide during their penalty corners and that made a huge difference.
Germany, however, did not look at their best in the opening stages. Their crosses often lacked precision, while heavy touches repeatedly disrupted their attacking moves and allowed Spain to threaten. In the end, however, the Germans did just enough to secure the win and retain their world title.
It was also heartbreak for Spain coach Max Caldas, who had previously lost a World Cup final in 2018 while coaching Netherlands. The Dutch side had gone down to Belgium in a shootout at Kalinga Stadium in Bhubaneswar.
Meanwhile, there was further heartbreak for Netherlands, who finished without a World Cup medal for the first time since 2006. They lost 1-2 to Argentina in the bronze-medal match earlier on Sunday.
